Maladaptive Strategies.value: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

vignette:
Mateo, a 22-year-old product manager who emigrated from Honduras with his family at age twelve, first came to therapy six months after a crisis at work had prompted his supervisor to suggest he take leave. What emerged was not a single event but a prolonged and embedded trauma. When he was sixteen, he had returned to his hometown for a summer visit, staying with his grandmother in a neighborhood that had, over the preceding year, fallen under the control of a local cartel. One evening, without warning, sustained automatic gunfire erupted three blocks away, followed by shouting, the sounds of running, and then a heavy silence that lasted hours. Mateo and his grandmother lay on the floor of a back bedroom, and through a gap in the curtain he saw a neighbor, a man he had known since childhood, lying motionless in the street. They remained in that room until dawn, and for the rest of the summer Mateo did not leave the house.

After returning to the United States, Mateo found that his body had not returned with him. He remained constantly tense, his shoulders locked and his jaw clenched, and he noticed that his heart would pound at sounds that other people did not even register - a car door slamming, a chair scraping the floor, footsteps approaching too quickly. In class, and later in his first job as an associate product manager, he sat with his back to the wall and monitored the room without intending to. What frightened him most was the way unexpected movement close to him would cause him to flinch so violently that others noticed, which embarrassed him and made him feel broken.

As the months passed, these physical states began to drive a set of behaviors that Mateo did not at first recognize as connected. When the tension in his body became unbearable - which happened daily, especially after a meeting in which a colleague had walked suddenly into his peripheral vision - he would go to the bathroom and press his fingernails into his forearms until the physical sting momentarily overrode the alarm in his chest. He had come to believe that if he did not release the pressure somehow, something catastrophic would happen: his body would simply break. At the same time, he found himself asking his roommate repeatedly whether he seemed okay, whether his face looked normal, whether his breathing was fast. He would check his own pulse throughout the day and examine his arms for scratches or bruises he might not have noticed, certain that any mark could be a sign of an injury he had failed to detect while on guard.

The problem, as Mateo described it with growing frustration, was that these strategies only seemed to make things worse. The more he checked his body, the more he noticed small sensations - a twitch, a throb, a flutter - and interpreted them as threats he needed to monitor. The more he asked his roommate for reassurance, the more he worried that his need to ask proved something was wrong. And the self-harm, though it brought a fleeting release, left him ashamed and more vigilant afterward, scanning his own skin for evidence of what he had done. By the time he sought help, his days had become a closed loop: his body stayed on alert, which drove him to strategies that fed the very vigilance he was trying to escape.

He could no longer sit through a full day at the office without needing to leave the floor at least twice, and his manager had noticed that he flinched during a team standup when a coworker reached past him for a marker. Mateo was referred to the employee assistance program, and from there to trauma-focused therapy. What he hoped for, he said, was simply to stop checking - to stop feeling like something was about to happen, to stop needing to hurt himself to feel still. But he was also afraid that if he stopped monitoring, he would miss the thing that was coming.
